text.p: These are the key facts about the North African state of Algeria, which on Thursday holds its first general election after five years of civil strife.
POPULATION: 28.8 million (April 1997) 75 percent under 30 years, of Arab and Berber stock.
LANGUAGES: Arab (official), French (widely spoken in cities), Berber (especially in Kabylie and Aures mountain regions, east and southeast of Algiers respectively).

AREA: 2,380,000 sq km (920,000 sq miles), most of it in Sahara desert. Bordering on Morocco and Western Sahara in the west, on Mauritania, Mali and Niger in the south, on Libya and Tunisia in the east, and on the Mediterranean in the north.

ARMED FORCES: Active - 121,700 men (90,000 conscripts), 960 tanks, 170 combat aircraft, including MiG-21s, MiG-23s), 60 armed helicopters, two submarines, three corvettes, 22 patrol and coastal craft. (SOURCE: International Institute for Strategic Studies - Military Balance 1995/96).
Paramilitary forces: gendarmerie force of 24,000, and 12,000 Republican Guard (Defence Ministry); 16,000 National Security Forces and more than 16,000 Communal Guards (Interior Ministry).

ECONOMY: Based on oil and gas. GDP (1996) $43.9 billion, against $35.1 billion in 1995 (source - Finance Minister Abdelkrim Harchaoui, March 1997). Against $34.5 billion in 1994, $46.3 billion in 1993 (source Central Bank). Minister's forecast for 1997 was $48.2 billion.

HISTORY: Algeria, formerly part of Ottoman Empire, invaded by France in 1830. Became colony with more than one million French settlers. Guerrilla war launched by National Liberation Front on November 1, 1954. Independence proclaimed on July 5, 1962.

Ahmed Ben Bella elected first president. Overthrown in 1965 by then Defence Minister Colonel Houari Boumedienne. Colonel Chadli Benjedid succeeded Boumedienne in 1979 after his death. Returned for five-year terms in 1984 and 1988. After nationwide youth riots in October 1988, Chadli promised multi-party democracy.

First round of general elections on December 26, 1991, gave fundamentalist Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) overwhelming lead. To take power it needed only 28 more seats from run-off voting set for January 16, 1992.

Chadli resigned on January 11, 1992. Diplomats said he was forced out by army officers. Half-finished election scrapped and five-man High Council of State set up as collective presidency, headed by Mohamed Boudiaf.

Authorities declared a state of emergency on February 9 and court ordered dissolution of FIS on March 4, 1992. More violence erupted. On June 29, Boudiaf was assassinated in the eastern town of Annaba. Ali Kafi took over as head of state.

Violence switched from street unrest to guerrilla attacks. In five years, about 60,000 people have been killed, including more than 100 foreigners, most of whose deaths have been attributed to the Armed Islamic Group. Killings have included ambushes, bombs in towns and cities, and massacres in isolated villages.
Retired general Liamine Zeroual appointed president after Kafi stepped down at end of 1994. Zeroual was returned to power in Algeria's first plural presidential poll in November 1995.
Drew up constitutional reforms approved in 1996 referendum, changed party laws to ban religion as a party platform. In January 1997, announced general elections would be held on June 5.
